title: Introduction to Vue.js
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Introduction to Vue.js in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Introduction to Vue.js within Introduction to Vue.js. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: A clear mental model helps you decide what belongs in Vue, what remains ordinary JavaScript, and when the framework is a good fit.

content_blocks.title: Introduction to Vue.js: Component communication
content_blocks.alt_text: Component communication diagram for lesson 1: Introduction to Vue.js. Parent owns the value or business intent → Child receives data and renders its view → Child emits intent; parent decides updates
content_blocks.caption: Component flow: data moves into children through props; emitted events communicate requested changes back to the owner.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Vue is a progressive JavaScript framework for building interfaces from declarative templates, reactive state, and reusable components. This lesson focuses on Introduction to Vue.js. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: What Vue.js is
items.text: For What Vue.js is, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Vue as a JavaScript framework
items.text: For Vue as a JavaScript framework, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Declarative rendering and reactive interfaces
items.text: For Declarative rendering and reactive interfaces, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Vue's component-based programming model
items.text: For Vue's component-based programming model, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

content_blocks.expected_output: The page displays “Hello, Vue!”; changing message.value in script updates the rendered text.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Place the excerpt in App.vue in a create-vue project, run npm run dev, and open the printed local URL.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Introduction to Vue.js with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Vue as a JavaScript framework”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Vue is a progressive JavaScript framework for building interfaces from declarative templates, reactive state, and reusable components. For Introduction to Vue.js, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Introduction to Vue.js” that applies “What Vue.js is”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “What Vue.js is”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Introduction to Vue.js belongs to the broader area Introduction to Vue.js.
The main concept to practice is What Vue.js is.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
